source.title: Scaling Laws and Efficient Inference for Ternary Language Models
source.authors: Tejas Vaidhya; Ayush Kaushal; Vineet Jain; Francis Couture-Harpin; Prashant Shishodia; Majid Behbahani; Yuriy Nevmyvaka; Irina Rish

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation loss across model parameter counts and training-token amounts, then fits a scaling law in the same general manner as the original scaling-law work, but on ternary models and a separate FloatLM suite.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fitted validation-loss laws and fit-quality statistics for TriLMs and FloatLMs. It also evaluates downstream benchmarks, but does not report a fitted or otherwise demonstrated predictive relationship between pretraining loss or scale and downstream performance. Inference-speed and packing results do not bear on the claim. Comparisons or results attributed to prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits the Hoffmann-style parametric loss law L(N,D)=E+A/N^α+B/D^β to final validation losses of a ternary (TriLM) sweep and a 16-bit (FloatLM) sweep. That is the same method and measure as the original, and it bears on V1 (power-law form fits) and V7 (exponents depend on setup, here weight precision). The ternary suite is also a new setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that TriLM loss falls faster with training tokens than with parameters, unlike FloatLMs where both exponents are similar, and that fitted constants and coefficients likely depend on quantization level. They also conclude that TriTera models trained to 1.2T tokens keep improving and are competitive with FloatLMs at a given compute budget.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a joint parameter-and-data validation-loss fit in the general form associated with prior scaling-law work, but applies it to ternary models and a separate 16-bit suite. The sweeps are limited in range and do not estimate a fixed-compute optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted coefficients and exponents differ between ternary and 16-bit model suites; the authors suggest quantization level may affect them.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The fitted sweeps cover less than several orders of magnitude in parameters and tokens. The reported R² values assess fits to the same suites used to estimate the coefficients; a held-out extrapolation test is not stated. The text also describes a changed learning-rate schedule and removal of weight decay relative to prior ternary training procedures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the scaling-law results.

untested.parts: Ranges of several orders of magnitude (only ~1 order in N and D); compute-axis scaling.
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs is tested. The 1.2T-token TriTera runs are not compared with law predictions.
No fixed-compute optimal N/D allocation is derived, although the exponent asymmetry implies one.
Architecture shape not varied at fixed N.
No other modalities, repeated data, or fine-tuning.
No quantitative test of downstream predictability from loss or scale. Figure 1 shows MMLU vs FLOPs fit lines without reported parameters.
Fitting method, parameter counting, schedule and data choices not varied; no curvature away from a power law examined.

missing.what: Figure 1 plots MMLU vs training FLOPs with 'TriTera Fit' and 'Spectra Fit' trend lines; no fit parameters or quality reported

record.verdict_notes: The 'limits_scope' label for range in the record was removed. The narrow range is an untested part of V1, not a qualification shown by results. The paper's main contributions (packing schemes, TriRun kernels) do not bear on the claim. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The sweeps cover 99M–1.1B parameters and 20–150 billion tokens for TriLMs, not several orders of magnitude. The 1.2-trillion-token runs are a separate extension and are not the basis of the fitted sweep.
The paper does not report fitting laws on small runs and using them to predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not optimize parameter and token allocation at fixed compute or fit compute-optimal growth trends.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The scaling-law experiments concern language-model pretraining; other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Downstream benchmarks are reported, but the study does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to pretraining loss or scale.

The study compares fitted laws for ternary and 16-bit models and notes possible dependence on quantization. It does not vary fitting method, parameter counting, schedule, or data to test their effects, does not test compute-optimal splits, and does not report curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: TriLM suite (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a joint function of parameter count N and training tokens D across a sweep of converged models.

conditions.value: number of training tokens in billions
SlimPajama subset for experiments at or below 150B tokens

rows.measure: Final validation loss; fitted scaling law
rows.note: The paper states that increasing tokens lowers validation loss more effectively than increasing parameters for TriLMs.
rows.check: Values match Eq. (2). Units are N in millions and D in billions, so coefficients are not directly comparable to Chinchilla's. The sweep spans about 11x in N (99M–1.1B) and 7.5x in D (20–150B), roughly one order of magnitude, not several.

rows.subject: FloatLM suite (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a joint function of parameter count N and training tokens D across a sweep of 16-bit models.
rows.measure: Final validation loss; fitted scaling law
rows.note: The authors report that the parameter and data exponents are nearly the same for FloatLMs, unlike the TriLM fit.
rows.check: Values match Eq. (3). The stated FloatLM sizes (990M–11000M) are exactly 10x the TriLM sizes, possibly a typo in the paper. The parameter range therefore differs from, or is uncertain relative to, the TriLM sweep, which confounds the precision comparison.

rows.subject: TriLM suite (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Report coefficient of determination for the fitted scaling law against the empirical validation losses.
rows.note: The fit is evaluated on the suite of models used to obtain the coefficients; a held-out fit assessment is not stated.
rows.check: In-sample R² on the same runs used to fit; no held-out check.

relationships.condition: TriLM and FloatLM pretraining sweeps, ~1 order of magnitude in N and D
relationships.reason: The Chinchilla-form power law fits final validation loss with R² 0.9921 (TriLM) and 0.9958 (FloatLM); r1–r4.
relationships.display_finding: Chinchilla-form fits achieved final validation-loss R² of 0.9921 for TriLM and 0.9958 for FloatLM.

relationships.reason: α/β are 0.32/0.81 for TriLM vs 0.56/0.53 for FloatLM, with markedly different constants; authors attribute this to quantization level (r1, r2). The comparison is partly confounded by possibly differing N ranges.
relationships.display_finding: TriLM yielded α/β of 0.32/0.81 versus FloatLM's 0.56/0.53, with substantially different constants, although potentially different model-size ranges partly confounded the precision comparison.
